newsitem.title: SWEDEN: Ex-Stockholm air cargo rate hikes seen unlikely.
newsitem.headline: Ex-Stockholm air cargo rate hikes seen unlikely.

text.p: Air cargo prices from Sweden were fairly steady but strong competition was seen blocking the usual round of rate increases due in the autumn, air freight forwarders and airlines said.
"The rates are very stable with a few exceptions," ASG Air & Sea traffic manager Goran Norell told Reuters.

However, due to the number of freighters operating from the Nordic region and less cargo on the market, airlines were unlikely to be able to raise their prices during the usual autumn round, players said.
"The competition has been harder. KLM has been on the offensive in the market and air cargo export volumes have gone down in general," Finnair Cargo spokesman Bengt Lundell said.
Asked about the possibility of price increases, Lundell said: "I don't think so, not from Scandinavia this year. That's because of the competition. There are so many freighters on the market."
British Airways cargo manager Sweden Anders Uddman said the British carrier was not planning any major moves.
"We are not planning any major price increases. There may be some variation because we also have to look at any currency alterations," Uddman told Reuters.
Mats Svensson, manager of freight forwarder Spedman's air cargo division, agreed there was less freight around at the moment to be shipped but said this would probably change.
"If you ask me again in a month I'll probably say there are some problems finding space," said Svensson.
Thai Airways International Scandinavia and Finland cargo sales manager Peter Sull said air cargo exports from Sweden were sluggish at the moment and saw them picking up only in 1997.
"In Sweden we really see a lower demand until the end of the year, but next year it should be better," Sull said.
The average market rate for a 100-kg shipment with a volume to weight ratio of six-to-one from Stockholm to New York was steady at 9.75 crowns compared to 9.70 crowns a month ago.
To Chicago the rate was flat at 11.30 crowns and to Los Angeles it was also unchanged at 12.70 crowns.
Finnair's Lundell said surface shipping may be attracting some shipments which otherwise would have gone by air across the Atlantic Ocean.
"There are very fast ships going from Gothenburg to New York in five to six days. I think air cargo has lost some of the market to surface transportation," Lundell said.

Rates to the far east, excluding Japan, were also steady. The average market rate from Stockholm to Hong Kong was 13.30 crowns a kg compared to 13.20 and to Singapore the rate was 13.30 crowns versus 13.40.
To Bangkok the rate fell to 13.00 crowns from 13.40, because of increased capacity, players said.
Prices to Japan dropped more sharply, to 19.40 crowns from 20 crowns.
"To Japan it's the SAS freighter that's pushing prices down. It always takes some time before the prices are affected," one freight forwarder said.

Another forwarder also said rates to Japan had fallen because of the SAS (Scandinavian Airlines System) Boeing 747-200 freighter, which has flown to Osaka from the Swedish west coast city Gothenburg twice weekly since April.
Available space to Sydney, which market players said cost around 24 crowns per kg, was in demand.
The most dramatic price fall was for space to Johannesburg, which slid to 20.60 crowns from 21.40.
"A new carrier came in and they have marked the level. I think the others will follow. Today I can buy freight for 19 crowns to Johannesburg no problem," one forwarder said.
The rate from Stockholm to London was steady at 7.70 crowns per kg compared to 7.90.

The average price per kg to Paris was lower, at 7.50 crowns compared to 8.00, with more airlines quoting a price substantially below the market average -- at six crowns per kg -- bringing the average down.
The price to Sao Paulo was 21.80 crowns compared to 22 crowns.
